g.text: Follows the data definition: first/rest, left/right.
Subproblems are computed, not parts of the data.
Two or more recursive calls per step.
Work deferred and done on the way back.
State carried down; nothing left to do on return.
A list whose rest is again a list.
A tree whose children are trees.
A pictorial object holding a smaller copy.
The call as written, concrete args.
Half-evaluated term, as in a trace.
Labelled or highlighted as the base case.
The last call is drawn but not singled out.
A failed branch ends the recursion.
Size n aligned to size n−1.
The decision named on the edge.
Dead branches, keyed in a legend.
Rule implied by a few levels.
The subcall’s result is used without drawing inside it (leap of faith).
Down to the base case, then back up.
Value written on the way back.
Every call’s result is shown coming back.
Only some results, e.g. the final one.
Calls only; for a recursive process the way back is missing.
Parametric size, as in a recurrence.
Cases of one step side by side.
Work done per call or level.
Trace written in the program’s own syntax.
Placed next to it, arrowed into
Structure and Interpretation of Computer Programs
Figure X: A design space for recursion diagrams. The recursion type is set by the problem; each recursion concept lists the ways it is drawn.
